name: fast_prng (cd-mcfarland modified ziggurat)
baseline: Doornik ziggurat normal and Marsaglia-Tsang ziggurat exponential (other ziggurat generators profiled in the repo); not std::normal_distribution or Boost
workload: Mean time per generated standard normal (and exponential) variate over 1e9 draws, uniform source is SFMT-based MT19937.h.
claimed_speedup: README example output: 'Mean execution time (per PRN): 7.987 (ns)' for 1e9 standard normal draws. The README page gives no baseline timing; benchmarks/ holds profile.c variants for Doornik normal and Marsaglia-Tsang/double Marsaglia exponential but no committed results file was found.
compiler_and_flags: README: gcc -O2 -DNORMAL profile.c -lm. benchmarks/profile_all.py default config: gcc-4.8 -O2, 5 trials, median.
hardware: README run: not stated. benchmarks/profile_all.py default CPU string: Intel Core i7-3770K @ 3.50GHz (other CPUs commented out).
stars_or_usage: 13 stars; algorithm ported to Apache Commons RNG (ZigguratSampler), USGS BiF Fortran lib, and cited by a pedrobtz/zurand method request
tradeoffs: Header-only C (normal.h, exponential.h, shared.h) with its own SFMT-derived MT19937.h as the uniform source; also Python (pip fast_prng), MATLAB/Octave bindings. Table-based ziggurat with global generator state; the README describes bug fixes by a contributor (rejection sampling and overhang indexing off by one) that moment tests did not detect.
caveats: The listed baselines (std::mt19937, PCG, xoshiro) are uniform generators, not normal samplers, so they do not fit this project; the real comparison is against other ziggurat implementations. No head-to-head against std::normal_distribution or Boost was found on pages opened. Paper (J. Stat. Comput. Simul. 86(7), 2016; arXiv 1403.6870) abstract says median runtimes of the new algorithm for exponential and normal variates are reduced to 58% and 53% (range 41-93%); this was seen only in a WebSearch result snippet because arxiv.org and tandfonline.com are blocked here (snippet only, not opened). The last commit only added a LICENSE file. Third-party PR pedrobtz/zurand#45 (opened) reports McFarland's method 1.02-1.25x faster than that package's default normal method and 'transform alone 21-39% faster per value on eight CPUs', which is a different baseline and not a std comparison. A timings.csv referenced by benchmarks/profile_all.py returned 404 at HEAD.
found_via: seed-record pass: https://github.com/cd-mcfarland/fast_prng README and benchmarks/profile.c, profile_all.py

name: MultiprecisionBenchmarks (dzhang314)
baseline: MPFR (equal-precision comparison against QD dd_real/qd_real, MultiFloats and other libraries); GMP also benchmarked
workload: Google Benchmark harness: axpy and dot (n 2^8..2^24), gemv (n 2^4..2^12) and gemm (n 2^3..2^9) at MPFR precisions 53, 103, 156, 208 bits versus QD dd_real/qd_real, plus GMP, CLN, FLINT, Boost, libquadmath, CAMPARY and MultiFloats; OMP thread counts 1-32 via bench_linux.sh.
claimed_speedup: No speedup claimed and no results committed or stated in the README (the README is only the title). The repo is a benchmark harness.
compiler_and_flags: Binaries built for GCC and Clang (bench_linux.sh runs *BenchmarkGCC and *BenchmarkClang); flags not stated in files opened (no Makefile at HEAD).
tradeoffs: Harness only: it is useful for measuring double-double and quad-double style fixed-width floating-point expansions against MPFR at the same bit precision, but it provides no library of its own other than the benchmark kernels (common/kernels.hpp, per-library main.cpp).
caveats: No committed benchmark outputs and no stated numbers, so no claim to verify; tier D. The author's MultiFloats library appears among the contenders, which makes this a self-benchmark if results are ever published. Fewer than 1k stars, so it is not notable under the tier D rule; recorded because the seed pass requires one record per project. Precision pairing seen in mpfr/main.cpp (53, 103, 156, 208 bits) and qd/main.cpp (dd_real, qd_real) is close to but not exactly equal precision (dd is ~106 bits, qd ~212 bits).
found_via: seed-record pass: https://github.com/dzhang314/MultiprecisionBenchmarks plus bench_linux.sh, qd/main.cpp, mpfr/main.cpp

name: SyLVER (NLAFET)
baseline: SPRAL SSIDS / HSL MA87 / PARDISO (no comparison found in the repo)
workload: Sparse symmetric positive-definite (Cholesky) and indefinite (LDL^T) direct factorization on multicore and GPU through the StarPU runtime; no benchmark in the repo.
claimed_speedup: None. The README and doc/source pages (purpose.rst, introduction.rst) describe DAG-based algorithms that 'enable an efficient exploitation of multicore CPU architectures and GPU-accelerated systems' with no numbers.
tradeoffs: Requires StarPU 1.3+, SPRAL (submodule), MeTiS, hwloc and a sequential BLAS/LAPACK (MKL or ESSL recommended); optional CUDA. Mixed C++ and Fortran 2003 sources (test drivers are .F90). Developed for the EU H2020 NLAFET project; last commit May 2020.
caveats: No numbers in README, doc/source or drivers (drivers hold only spldlt_test.F90, spldlt_test_debug.F90, splu_test.F90). NLAFET deliverable and working-note PDFs on www.nlafet.eu (for example WN21 Duff-Hogg-Lopez on sparse Cholesky with a task-flow implementation) were returned by WebSearch but nlafet.eu is blocked here, so no paper numbers were read. SyLVER is the StarPU-based successor of SPRAL SSIDS, so SPRAL SSIDS is its natural baseline, and that is a library also listed under this category by other entries. Language label is inferred from the file listing (src/, include/sylver, Fortran drivers); the GitHub language bar was not shown.
found_via: seed-record pass: https://github.com/NLAFET/SyLVER README, doc/source, drivers directory and WebSearch for SyLVER vs SPRAL/PARDISO papers

name: OGL (hpsim, OpenFOAM Ginkgo Layer)
baseline: OpenFOAM native CPU linear solvers (PCG and similar); not SuiteSparse, Eigen sparse or PETSc
workload: OpenFOAM pressure/momentum linear solves offloaded to Ginkgo CG, BiCGStab, GMRES with block-Jacobi/ISAI/ILU/IC/multigrid preconditioners on CUDA, HIP, SYCL or OpenMP executors; the paper reports GPU versus CPU OpenFOAM timings.
claimed_speedup: No timings on the README. Benchmark data for OGL and Ginkgo versions on several machines is archived in https://github.com/hpsim/OGL_DATA (CSV plus OpenFOAM logs, produced by the OBR scripts), but no summary figures were read from it.
stars_or_usage: 41 stars, 14 forks; cited as the Ginkgo backend for OpenFOAM in the Meccanica 2024 paper
tradeoffs: Thin plugin over Ginkgo (https://github.com/ginkgo-project/ginkgo), fetched and built by CMake; needs OpenFOAM 6+ or v2106 and a C++17 compiler. Limitations per README: only basic cyclic boundary conditions, no AMI, no block-coupled matrices; ILU, IC, multigrid and Ell/Hybrid formats experimental. Host-device copies of the matrix each solve unless updateRHS is changed.
caveats: OGL contains no solver kernels of its own, so it is largely a Ginkgo wrapper and probably should fold into the existing Ginkgo entry as a duplicate or integration. The only performance figure found is a WebSearch snippet of the Meccanica paper (Olenik, Koch, Boutanios, Anzt, doi 10.1007/s11012-024-01806-1) saying the largest GPU-versus-CPU speedup was about 15x on one machine and speedup grows with problem size; link.springer.com is blocked here so the paper was not opened (snippet only), and the CPU baseline solver, compiler and hardware are unknown. Tier set to C because the numbers could not be checked on an opened page. License: README SPDX header is GPL-3.0-or-later and LICENSES/ also holds MIT and Unlicense texts (REUSE layout), so some files carry different terms.
found_via: seed-record pass: https://github.com/hpsim/OGL README, https://github.com/hpsim/OGL_DATA README, and WebSearch for the OGL Meccanica paper
